newsitem.title: UK: UK's Imperial set for 370-380p share price.
newsitem.headline: UK's Imperial set for 370-380p share price.

text.p: Shares in Britain's second largest tobacco company, Imperial Tobacco, one of the four new firms created from the demerger of Hanson Plc, are expected to start trading on Tuesday at 370-380p.

The price is likely to be lower than at first anticipated because of the legal action launched by a group of 40 cancer sufferers on Friday against Imperial Tobacco and American Brands Inc unit Gallaher.
"The uncertainty is what the Americans are going to do given the bad publicity surrounding the litigation proceedings," said Ian Rennardson, an analyst at Credit Lyonnais.
About 30 percent of Hanson shares are owned by U.S.-based investors who may be more worried by the "no win, no fee" basis that lawyers for the plaintiffs are now prepared to work on.
A flurry of lawsuits would mean higher defence costs for tobacco firms, analysts said.
On a prospective dividend of 21p for next year and a price of 375p the shares would show a fair yield of seven percent and reflect the risk of lawsuits, they said.
Imperial Tobacco generates mountains of cash and is viewed as one of the most efficient cigarette companies in the world.

The group's net cash inflow represented some 99 percent of operating profit in the five-year period ended September 30, 1995. Most of the group's post-tax profit is therefore available to repay debt, finance future growth and provide returns to shareholders.

Net cash inflow last year was 368 million and its capital expenditure requirements have been low at 5.0 percent of net cash inflow. In the nine months to June 30 it achieved an eight percent increase in turnover and operating profit to 2.8 billion and 270 million stg respectively. Return on sales is about 46 percent.

Although the total UK cigarette market fell from 95 billion cigarettes in 1991 to 83 billion in 1995, Imperial has managed to maintain its sales by increasing its market share from under 33 percent in September 1990 to its current 38 percent.
The company's only factory in Nottingham is installing machines capable of turning out 16,000 cigarettes a minute, 60 percent faster than machines it has at present.
"So there are major productivity benefits yet to come through with Imperial," said Charles Pick, an analyst at Panmure Gordon.

But if the company is to show more lasting long-term growth it will need to expand into the emerging markets of China, Russia and Asia where the likes of B.A.T Industries have a strong grip, analysts said.

But it has already had some success overseas, making good inroads into French domestic duty-free markets with its John Player brand. Overseas profits increased by about 45 percent to 45 million stg last year.
